title: Hippocampal sclerosis, Alzheimer disease and amnesia
text:
The hippocampus is one of the first regions to show neurofibrillary tangles and atrophy in Alzheimer disease, causing early loss of new episodic memory. CA1 pyramidal neurons (Sommer sector) are exquisitely sensitive to hypoxia, so cardiac arrest can leave isolated anterograde amnesia.
Mesial temporal (hippocampal) sclerosis is the commonest cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy in adults, often after prolonged febrile seizures in childhood, and can be cured by anterior temporal lobectomy. Bilateral hippocampal removal (patient H.M.) abolished the formation of new declarative memories. HSV encephalitis also targets the medial temporal lobes.

title: Klüver-Bucy syndrome and fear processing
text: Bilateral damage to the amygdalae (HSV encephalitis, trauma, frontotemporal dementia) produces Klüver-Bucy syndrome: placidity with loss of fear, hyperorality, hypersexuality and visual agnosia. Selective bilateral calcification in Urbach-Wiethe disease abolishes fear recognition. Seizures arising in the amygdala produce an epigastric 'rising' sensation and fear.

title: Huntington disease
text: An autosomal dominant CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene (with anticipation, especially through paternal transmission) causes loss of GABAergic medium spiny neurons, first in the caudate. Atrophy of the caudate heads enlarges the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles ('boxcar' ventricles). Loss of the indirect pathway disinhibits movement: chorea, followed by dementia, depression and psychiatric illness, typically beginning in the 30s to 40s.

title: Parkinsonism, hypertensive haemorrhage and Wilson disease
text:
Loss of dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra to the putamen causes Parkinson disease: resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability. Deep brain stimulation of the internal globus pallidus or subthalamic nucleus relieves symptoms.
The putamen is the commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage, from rupture of the lenticulostriate arteries (Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms), often extending into the internal capsule with dense contralateral hemiplegia.
Copper deposition in Wilson disease, and bilateral globus pallidus necrosis in carbon monoxide poisoning, selectively damage the lentiform nucleus.

title: Thalamic stroke and Dejerine-Roussy syndrome
text:
Lacunar infarction of the ventral posterolateral nucleus (thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery) causes pure contralateral sensory loss. Weeks later, some patients develop agonising burning pain and allodynia in the numb area (thalamic pain syndrome).
Occlusion of the artery of Percheron, a single artery supplying both paramedian thalami, causes sudden coma or hypersomnolence with vertical gaze palsy. Thiamine deficiency (Wernicke-Korsakoff) damages the medial dorsal thalamic nuclei and mammillary bodies.

title: Hypothalamic lesions
text: The hypothalamus integrates endocrine and autonomic control, so damage produces a characteristic mix: diabetes insipidus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei), hyperphagia and obesity (ventromedial nucleus), anorexia (lateral nucleus), hypothermia or hyperthermia, and disrupted sleep-wake cycles (suprachiasmatic nucleus). Craniopharyngioma and germinoma are typical tumours. Hypothalamic hamartomas cause gelastic (laughing) seizures and precocious puberty.

title: Midbrain syndromes
text:
Weber syndrome (paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery): ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis from the cerebral peduncle.
Benedikt syndrome: oculomotor palsy with contralateral tremor and ataxia from involvement of the red nucleus.
Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome: pineal tumours or hydrocephalus compress the superior colliculi and pretectum, causing upward gaze palsy, light-near dissociation of the pupils, convergence-retraction nystagmus and eyelid retraction.
The substantia nigra pars compacta, in the midbrain, degenerates in Parkinson disease.

title: Locked-in syndrome and central pontine myelinolysis
text:
Basilar artery occlusion infarcting the ventral pons destroys the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts bilaterally while sparing the reticular activating system: the patient is fully conscious but quadriplegic and mute, communicating only by vertical eye movements and blinking (locked-in syndrome).
Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination of the central pons, leading to quadriparesis, dysarthria and dysphagia days later.
Pontine haemorrhage produces coma with pinpoint pupils and hyperthermia.

title: Lateral and medial medullary syndromes
text:
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, from vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion: ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus), contralateral body pain and temperature loss (spinothalamic tract), dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo and nystagmus (vestibular nuclei), ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ataxia. Motor function is spared.
Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery): contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid), contralateral loss of proprioception (medial lemniscus) and ipsilateral tongue deviation (hypoglossal nerve).
Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses the medullary respiratory and cardiovascular centres, causing apnoea and death.

title: Cerebellar syndromes and Chiari malformation
text:
Hemisphere lesions cause IPSILATERAL limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, past-pointing and hypotonia; vermis lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia (alcohol-related degeneration of the anterior superior vermis produces a wide-based gait with relatively normal arms). Nodular (flocculonodular) lesions such as medulloblastoma in children cause truncal ataxia and nystagmus. Cerebellar haemorrhage or infarct swelling can rapidly compress the fourth ventricle and brainstem.
Chiari I malformation: the cerebellar tonsils descend through the foramen magnum, causing occipital headache on coughing and syringomyelia. Chiari II adds herniation of the vermis and brainstem and is associated with myelomeningocele.

title: Motor cortex and frontal lobe lesions
text:
The primary motor cortex is organised as a homunculus: the leg area lies on the medial surface (anterior cerebral artery territory) and the face and arm areas laterally (middle cerebral artery territory). Jacksonian seizures 'march' along adjacent body parts. A transient postictal weakness is Todd paresis.
Prefrontal damage (trauma, frontotemporal dementia, tumours such as olfactory groove meningioma, or Phineas Gage's tamping iron) produces disinhibition, impulsivity, apathy, perseveration and primitive reflexes, sometimes with anosmia. Frontal eye field seizures drive the eyes away from the lesion; destructive lesions make them look toward it.

title: Broca aphasia
text: Lesions of Broca's area (usually the dominant left hemisphere, superior division of the middle cerebral artery) cause non-fluent, effortful, telegraphic speech with relatively preserved comprehension and impaired repetition. Patients are aware of and frustrated by their deficit. Contralateral face and arm weakness frequently coexists because the motor cortex is nearby.

title: Wernicke aphasia and temporal lobe lesions
text:
Damage to Wernicke's area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (inferior division of the middle cerebral artery) causes fluent but meaningless speech with neologisms and paraphasias, poor comprehension and repetition, and typically no awareness of the deficit. Conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus) impairs repetition alone.
Temporal lobe lesions also cause a contralateral upper quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky') by interrupting Meyer's loop of the optic radiation, and uncal herniation of the medial temporal lobe compresses the oculomotor nerve and midbrain.

title: Parietal lobe syndromes: neglect and Gerstmann syndrome
text:
Non-dominant (usually right) parietal lesions cause hemispatial neglect of the left side of space and body, anosognosia (denial of deficit) and dressing apraxia.
Dominant parietal lesions near the angular gyrus produce Gerstmann syndrome: finger agnosia, left-right confusion, acalculia and agraphia.
Postcentral gyrus lesions cause cortical sensory loss: impaired two-point discrimination, stereognosis and graphaesthesia with preserved primary sensation. Parietal lesions of the optic radiation give an inferior quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor').

title: Cortical blindness and macular sparing
text:
Posterior cerebral artery occlusion infarcts the visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus, producing a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing because the occipital pole also receives middle cerebral artery collaterals. Bilateral occipital infarction (top-of-the-basilar embolus) causes cortical blindness, sometimes with denial of blindness (Anton syndrome).
The cuneus above the calcarine sulcus represents the lower visual field; the lingual gyrus below represents the upper field.

title: Callosal disconnection
text:
Section of the corpus callosum (surgical callosotomy for drop attacks, anterior cerebral artery infarction, Marchiafava-Bignami disease in alcohol use) disconnects the hemispheres: the patient cannot name objects felt in the left hand (tactile anomia), and the left hand may act independently (alien hand syndrome).
Glioblastoma can cross the callosum to form a 'butterfly' lesion. Callosal agenesis is associated with several developmental syndromes; multiple sclerosis plaques perpendicular to the callosum are 'Dawson fingers'.

title: Insular stroke and seizures
text: The insula lies deep to the Sylvian fissure and is supplied by M2 branches of the middle cerebral artery. Loss of the grey-white distinction over the insula ('insular ribbon sign') is an early CT sign of MCA infarction. Insular damage causes disturbed taste, autonomic instability and cardiac arrhythmias, and can abolish the urge to smoke. Insular seizures mimic frontal or temporal seizures, with throat constriction and visceral sensations.

title: Middle cerebral artery stroke
text: The commonest site of embolic stroke. Proximal M1 occlusion causes contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss affecting the face and arm more than the leg, homonymous hemianopia and gaze deviation toward the lesion, plus aphasia (dominant hemisphere) or neglect (non-dominant). Lenticulostriate branches from M1 supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia. Large MCA infarcts swell over 2 to 5 days ('malignant MCA syndrome') and may need decompressive craniectomy. Mechanical thrombectomy benefits large-vessel occlusions.

title: Anterior cerebral artery stroke and aneurysm
text:
Occlusion affects the medial frontal and parietal lobes: contralateral weakness and sensory loss of the LEG more than the arm, urinary incontinence, abulia and alien hand syndrome.
The anterior communicating artery is the commonest site of berry aneurysm; rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage ('worst headache of my life'), and an unruptured aneurysm can compress the optic chiasm. Rupture may damage the basal forebrain, causing memory problems and confabulation.

title: Vertebrobasilar ischaemia and berry aneurysms
text:
Basilar artery thrombosis causes fluctuating brainstem signs progressing to coma or locked-in syndrome; it carries a high mortality without recanalisation. Vertebral artery dissection (neck manipulation, sport) presents with occipital headache and lateral medullary syndrome.
Subclavian steal: a proximal subclavian stenosis reverses flow in the vertebral artery when the arm exercises, causing vertigo and syncope.
Berry aneurysms form at branching points of the circle of Willis (anterior communicating, posterior communicating and middle cerebral bifurcation) and are associated with polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and coarctation. Rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage, later vasospasm and hydrocephalus.

title: Hydrocephalus
text:
Obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus results from blocked CSF flow: colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro (sudden positional headache, can cause sudden death), aqueductal stenosis, posterior fossa tumours compressing the fourth ventricle, or Dandy-Walker malformation (atresia of the fourth ventricle outlets).
Communicating hydrocephalus follows impaired absorption at the arachnoid granulations after meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage. Normal pressure hydrocephalus in the elderly causes the triad of gait apraxia ('magnetic gait'), urinary incontinence and dementia ('wet, wobbly and wacky') and may improve with shunting.
Choroid plexus papillomas in children overproduce CSF.

title: Pineal tumours
text: Germinomas and pineoblastomas in the pineal region compress the tectum (Parinaud syndrome: upward gaze palsy, light-near dissociation) and the cerebral aqueduct, causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Germ cell tumours here may secrete beta-hCG and cause precocious puberty in boys. Pineal calcification is a common normal finding in adults and serves as a midline marker on imaging.

title: Spinal cord syndromes
text:
Brown-Séquard (hemisection): ipsilateral paralysis and loss of proprioception/vibration below the lesion, contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning one or two segments below.
Central cord syndrome (hyperextension in cervical spondylosis, syringomyelia): cape-like loss of pain and temperature across the shoulders and arms more than legs, as the crossing spinothalamic fibres and medially placed arm fibres are damaged first.
Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery occlusion, e.g. aortic surgery): paraplegia and loss of pain/temperature, with preserved dorsal columns.
Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency, nitrous oxide) damages dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts; tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis) damages dorsal columns and roots, causing sensory ataxia, a positive Romberg sign and Charcot joints.

title: Poliomyelitis, spinal muscular atrophy and ALS
text: Destruction of anterior horn cells produces pure lower motor neurone signs: flaccid weakness, wasting, fasciculations and areflexia without sensory loss. Poliovirus causes asymmetric acute paralysis; spinal muscular atrophy (SMN1 deletion) produces 'floppy baby' syndrome (Werdnig-Hoffmann). Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis combines anterior horn cell loss with lateral corticospinal tract degeneration, giving mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs and sparing eye movements and sphincters.

title: Cauda equina syndrome
text:
The spinal cord ends at L1/L2 in adults, so a lumbar puncture at L3/L4 or L4/L5 (level of the iliac crests) passes between floating roots of the cauda equina. Compression of these roots by a large central disc herniation, tumour, abscess or haematoma causes bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention with overflow incontinence, faecal incontinence and sexual dysfunction. It is a surgical emergency; delay leads to permanent sphincter loss.
Conus medullaris lesions produce similar but more symmetric deficits with earlier sphincter involvement and upper motor neurone signs.

title: Lumbar disc herniation
text:
Degeneration of the anulus fibrosus lets the nucleus pulposus herniate posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is thinnest. In the lumbar spine, a posterolateral herniation compresses the nerve root exiting at the level BELOW: an L4/L5 disc affects L5 (weak great toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion, numb dorsum of foot), an L5/S1 disc affects S1 (weak plantarflexion, lost ankle reflex, numb lateral foot). A far-lateral herniation compresses the root exiting at the same level.
Sciatica is reproduced by the straight leg raise test. Large central herniations can cause cauda equina syndrome.

title: Cervical radiculopathy and myelopathy
text:
In the cervical spine, root numbering changes: the C6 root exits above the C6 vertebra, so a C5/C6 disc compresses C6 (weak elbow flexion and wrist extension, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, numb thumb) and a C6/C7 disc compresses C7 (weak triceps, lost triceps reflex, numb middle finger).
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy from osteophytes and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy narrows the canal, causing clumsy hands, gait disturbance, hyperreflexia and a positive Hoffmann sign.

title: Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis
text: A stress fracture of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis), most often at L5 in gymnasts, fast bowlers and divers, shows as the 'Scottie dog collar' on oblique radiographs. Bilateral defects allow the vertebral body to slip forward on S1 (isthmic spondylolisthesis), producing back pain, hamstring tightness and L5 radiculopathy. Degenerative spondylolisthesis, typically at L4/L5 in older women, causes lumbar canal stenosis with neurogenic claudication relieved by sitting or bending forward.

title: Vertebral osteomyelitis, Pott disease and ankylosing spondylitis
text:
Haematogenous infection (Staphylococcus aureus; intravenous drug users; Batson's venous plexus from pelvic infection) begins in the vertebral endplates and spreads across the disc, destroying two adjacent vertebrae. Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) favours the thoracic spine, spares the disc early, causes anterior wedge collapse with a gibbus and may form a cold psoas abscess.
Ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27) starts at the sacroiliac joints and ascends, with syndesmophytes creating a 'bamboo spine' that fractures easily after minor trauma.

title: Horner syndrome
text:
Interruption of the three-neurone oculosympathetic pathway causes ipsilateral partial ptosis (Müller muscle), miosis, apparent enophthalmos and, in lesions before the carotid bifurcation, anhidrosis of the face.
First-order (central): lateral medullary syndrome, syringomyelia. Second-order (preganglionic): Pancoast tumour at the lung apex, neck surgery or trauma, cervical rib. Third-order (postganglionic): internal carotid dissection, cavernous sinus lesions, cluster headache.
A stellate ganglion block or thoracic sympathectomy (for hyperhidrosis or Raynaud phenomenon) deliberately produces the same signs.

title: Adrenal disease: phaeochromocytoma, Addison and Conn
text:
Adrenal medulla: phaeochromocytoma (chromaffin cells) causes episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension; associated with MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau and NF1. Neuroblastoma is the childhood medullary tumour.
Adrenal cortex: Conn syndrome (aldosterone-producing adenoma of the zona glomerulosa) causes hypertension with hypokalaemia; Cushing syndrome from a zona fasciculata adenoma; Addison disease (autoimmune destruction, tuberculosis) causes fatigue, hypotension, hyperkalaemia and hyperpigmentation from raised ACTH/POMC. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal septicaemia.
The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein; the short right adrenal vein enters the IVC directly, which makes right adrenalectomy more hazardous.
